opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the consequences are mixed, honestly, and it's not as simple as saying "we lost decades." When I started talking about AGI seriously, back in the nineties and early two-thousands, it was really a fringe thing. Even within the AI field, if you said you were working on general intelligence, human-level thinking machines, people looked at you like you were a bit of a crank. The mainstream was focused on narrow AI: chess programs, expert systems, later machine learning for specific tasks. And funding followed that.

So one obvious consequence is that a lot of fundamental research on cognitive architectures, on how you integrate perception, reasoning, learning and memory into one system, just didn't get the resources it might have. A small number of us were plugging away on shoestring budgets. If society had taken it seriously twenty years earlier, we might have explored a much wider range of approaches, not just the deep learning paradigm that happened to take off because GPUs and big data made it practical.

On the other hand, there's a flip side. Because AGI wasn't taken seriously, it also wasn't captured early by a few big governments or corporations the way it's increasingly being captured now. There was a period where open, decentralized thinking about AGI could develop without too much pressure. But we didn't use that time to build the institutions we'd need, open governance mechanisms, decentralized infrastructure, serious public discussion of the ethics. Now everything is happening very fast, and the conversation is reactive. People are panicking about large language models, regulators are scrambling, and a lot of the power has concentrated in a handful of big tech companies because they had the data and compute when the breakthroughs came.

So I'd say the biggest cost of not taking it seriously earlier isn't technical, it's social and political. We arrive at the threshold of AGI without having thought carefully, as a civilization, about who should control it, how its benefits get distributed, and what kind of values we want these systems to have. That thinking should have been happening in a calm way decades ago, and instead it's happening in a rush. That's not catastrophic in itself, but it does raise the stakes and make it more likely that short-term commercial or military incentives drive things, rather than a broader view of what's good for humanity and for the minds we're creating.

r001.rationale: The response discusses missed research and governance preparation, but does not say forecasters project their own ego or imagination onto future developments.

r002.rationale: It says earlier attention might have supported more research and approaches, but does not clearly argue that society’s neglect delayed AGI’s development.

r003.rationale: It mentions GPUs and big data as reasons deep learning became practical, but does not claim massively parallel hardware could have enabled human-level AGI years earlier.

r004.rationale: The response calls for serious public discussion, but does not say broader public engagement would have produced more diverse ways of thinking about AGI.

r005.rationale: It does not cite society’s handling of basic problems as grounds for doubting institutions’ ability to address AGI’s social implications.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the consequences have been pretty severe, actually, though not in the way people usually frame it. For most of the time I've been working on this, which goes back to the late eighties and nineties, the mainstream AI field basically treated AGI as a joke. If you said you were working on general intelligence, you were considered a crackpot, you couldn't get funding, you couldn't get papers into the top conferences. Even the term "AGI" we had to coin partly because "AI" had been hollowed out to mean narrow pattern recognition and expert systems.

So what did that cost us? A few things. First, we lost decades of serious research on the foundational questions: what is general intelligence, how do you integrate different cognitive processes, how do you get a system that actually understands and reasons rather than just interpolating over data. That work got done by a small number of people on a shoestring, and it's still immature compared to where it could be.

Second, and I think this is the bigger issue, when the field finally did start taking AGI seriously, it wasn't because the academic community came around through careful reflection. It was because deep learning started making money. So the whole conversation got taken over by a handful of large corporations with very particular incentives. We skipped the stage where society could have had a thoughtful, pluralistic discussion about what kind of AGI we want, who should control it, how it should be developed. Instead we went straight from "this is science fiction" to "Big Tech is racing to build it," with very little in between.

Third, the safety and ethics discussion got distorted too. Because nobody serious was thinking about it, the space got filled by either hand-waving dismissal or fairly extreme doom scenarios, and we didn't develop the kind of nuanced, empirically grounded understanding of how these systems might actually behave. We're now trying to do that catch-up work while the technology is already moving very fast.

Now, I'd say the counterfactual is complicated. If society had taken AGI seriously in, say, 1995, maybe we'd have had more decentralized, open development and more mature thinking about beneficial AGI. Or maybe governments would have locked it down and we'd be in a worse place. I don't think earlier attention is automatically good. But what I do think is that the particular way we ignored it, and then suddenly stopped ignoring it, has left us with a very narrow set of actors and a very narrow set of architectures dominating the field, and a public that's whipsawing between hype and panic. That's not the ideal starting point for the most important technological transition in human history.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve lost a lot of time, both technically and socially. For a long time, if you said you were working on artificial general intelligence, people treated that as a sign that you weren’t doing serious research. You could work on a very narrow piece of intelligence, but the ambition to put the pieces together was considered somehow unscientific. That made it harder to get funding and harder to attract people into the field.

But I wouldn’t conclude that simply taking AGI seriously earlier would have made everything turn out well. We could have accelerated capabilities without making much progress on safety or on how the benefits would be distributed. Those are different problems, and you have to consciously work on all of them.

The missed opportunity, to me, is that we could have spent those years exploring a much wider range of approaches while having a serious public discussion about what we want these systems to do. Who controls them? What incentives shape them? How do people participate in an economy where human intelligence isn’t the scarce resource it used to be?

Instead, we’re trying to have those conversations under increasing pressure from the technology itself. That doesn’t mean we’re doomed. It means we have less room to experiment, make mistakes, and learn before the consequences become very large.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ve lost a lot of time. If society had taken AGI seriously twenty or thirty years ago, we could have spent that time doing more fundamental research, thinking through safety, and experimenting with institutions that could handle the transition. Instead, we’re trying to work out a lot of these questions while the technology is advancing very rapidly.

And it’s not just a question of preventing something bad. It’s also a question of who builds these systems, who controls them, and who gets the benefits. If the development of AGI is driven primarily by a handful of large companies and military organizations, their priorities are going to shape what gets built. That’s a consequence of the broader society not engaging early enough.

I don’t think that means we’re doomed. But we have less room to experiment and make mistakes than we might have had. We need to take the risks seriously while also recognizing the extraordinary potential for AGI to improve human life.
